title: Crappy Antibodies, Made Superficially More Appealing
body_text: There have been reports for a while now about altered images of Western blots in the catalogs of various antibody suppliers, and this news (sadly) will not have come as a real shock to many of their customers. The state of the commercial antibody market has always been a shambles, as far back as I’ve been aware of it. There are antibodies from different catalogs that are actually the same thing, repackaged. And there are antibodies from suppliers that your employer may not even do business with (one in particular stands out, both for animal welfare issues as well as quality control). Then there are the ones that just flat out don’t work, no matter what the label or catalog might say. Have a look at this large-scale assessment from 2023, which found (among other things) that about half the commercially available antibodies they tested fail in one or more applications where you would have expected them to work. The authors in that case noted that “The hundreds of underperforming antibodies identified in this study were found to have been used in a large number of published articles, which should raise alarm.”, but also were able to get some manufacturers to take action. Well, it’s time for more action, guys. Reese Richardson at Northwestern has searched through thousands of images on the sites of 16 antibody vendors, and found over 18,000 instances that appear to be manipulated. He has helpfully put these into an open database, and the table of companies there is quite a sight. Santa Cruz, whose reputation is not high, has 111 affected products, but Thermo Fisher has 4,819, and G-Biosciences has 6,373 (!) That ain’t good. It would be useful to know how many of the underlying antibodies themselves are problematic, but if the images backing them up have already been hocused, you have to think that the odds of trouble are substantially increased. And besides, you’re not supposed to do this! I understand that they’re trying to sell product here, but you really owe your scientific customers the truth. As Nature reports, Thermo Fisher says that they stand by their data, but also say that the images might have been “edited, optimized, or otherwise adjusted”. I really like that “optimized”, which to me means “optimized to make people more likely to buy the stuff”. That article features a simultaneously infuriating and grimly amusing animation created by Richardson showing Western blots for over a hundred antibodies, one by one, each with its own distinct band. . .against the same damn noise background with every speckle intact. Which of course Does Not Happen. The Only Good Antibodies site has been trying to validate as many widely-used reagents as they can, and they have a valuable database that can be searched by gene or by vendor catalog numbers. I believe that at present there are over 1,600 of them that have been validated, but when you look at those numbers above it shows you that there’s a long way to go. “Caveat Blottor” does not seem like such a great way to run a business, but that seems to be the norm. Shouldn’t there be room for a company that is more willing to stand behind its reagents and more willing to show you real images of their behavior?
